beats.intro: Lesson nine. [[sub]]Staff meetings, operation reviews, and meetings called to make a decision.
beats.staff: A staff meeting brings a manager and all their reports together. [[peers]]Its special value is peer interaction. Deciding as a group of peers is hard, but it is central to good management, and the staff meeting is where people learn it. [[oppose]]The manager learns too: hearing two people argue opposite views teaches more than hearing one side. [[lab]]Grove learned this running a small research group, where the engineers often knew each other's work better than he did.
beats.staffwhat: What belongs in a staff meeting? [[two]]Anything that affects more than two of the people present. [[break]]If two people drift into a problem that concerns only them, break it off, and suggest they continue later. [[agenda]]Keep it mostly controlled, with an agenda sent out early enough to prepare. [[open]]But add an open session, where anyone can raise anything, from housekeeping to a first look at a big issue.
beats.role: And your role? [[roles]]Leader, observer, expediter, questioner, decision-maker. All of them. [[lect]]But never lecturer. Pontificating is the surest way to kill free discussion. [[chart]]Your effort should go into keeping the discussion on track, [[subs]]while your reports do the heavy work on the issues. [[family]]Staff meetings suit decisions, because everyone knows each other, like a family at dinner rather than strangers.
beats.opreview: Operation reviews bring together people who rarely meet. [[pres]]Managers present their work to their boss's boss, and to peers from other groups. [[purpose]]The purpose is teaching and learning across several levels. [[junior]]Junior people get comments and suggestions from senior ones. [[senior]]Senior people get a feel for the details. [[motiv]]And presenters are motivated to make a good impression.
beats.organizer: Each player has a job. [[org]]The organizer, usually the presenters' manager, picks the issues and the level of detail, handles the room and the invitations, [[time]]and keeps time, with quiet signals so nobody runs out halfway through their points. [[rev]]The reviewing manager, the senior person, asks questions, makes comments, and sets the spirit. [[prev]]He should never preview the material, so his reactions stay spontaneous. He is a role model for everyone in the room.
beats.presenters: Presenters should use visuals: in Grove's day, overhead transparencies; today, slides. [[eyes]]People take in more with eyes and ears together. [[flip]]But don't get so busy flipping charts that the message is lost. [[four]]Grove's rule of thumb: about four minutes per visual, including discussion. [[watch]]Highlight what matters, and watch the audience like a hawk. [[aud]]The audience has a job too: ask, object, and correct factual errors on the record. [[yawn]]Yawning or reading is worse than staying away. Attending is work.
beats.q2: Quick check. Whose job is it?
beats.mission: Mission-oriented meetings are called to produce one output, often a decision. [[chair]]Success depends on the chairman, the person with the most at stake, [[before]]and most of his work happens before the meeting starts. [[blame]]If the meeting fails, the chairman is to blame. [[want]]So know the objective. If you don't know what you want, you won't get it. [[three]]Then ask: is a meeting necessary? Desirable? Justifiable? Unless all three are yes, don't call it.
beats.cost: Meetings are expensive. [[rate]]Grove estimated a manager's time, with overhead, at about a hundred dollars an hour, in 1983. [[ten]]Ten managers for two hours: two thousand dollars. [[approve]]Most two-thousand-dollar purchases need a senior signature. A meeting can be called on a whim. [[invite]]So even as an invitee, ask whether it is justified. [[early]]If not, get it cancelled early, at the low-value stage, and use a cheaper medium: a one-on-one, a call, a note.
beats.q3: Quick check. Work out the cost.
beats.chair: The chairman has duties. [[who]]Decide who must attend, and get firm commitments. Anyone who cannot come sends someone who can speak for them. [[size]]Keep it small: six or seven people for a decision, [[eight]]eight at the absolute most. Decision-making is not a spectator sport. [[late]]And enforce punctuality. Letting someone waste everyone's time is like letting them walk off with two thousand dollars of equipment.
beats.agenda: Send an agenda that states the purpose and each person's role. [[ex]]Grove's example: a two-hour meeting to decide where to expand a plant in the Philippines. [[slots]]Manufacturing considerations, then construction considerations, then the alternatives with a preferred choice, then open discussion, each led by a named role. [[sarge]]It can feel like a drill sergeant. [[or]]But Grove, as a patient, would much rather have a disciplined operating room.
beats.minutes: Afterwards, send minutes, quickly, before people forget. [[what]]What was discussed, what was decided, [[who]]what is to be done, by whom, and by when. [[lev]]If the meeting was worth calling, this small extra effort has high leverage: it makes sure the meeting pays off.
beats.ratio: Ideally, regular process meetings would handle everything. [[eighty]]In practice, they handle maybe eighty percent of issues. [[twenty]]The other twenty percent need mission meetings. [[druck]]Drucker said spending more than a quarter of your time in meetings is a sign of poor organization. [[grove]]Grove puts it differently: the real warning sign is spending more than a quarter of your time in ad hoc, mission-oriented meetings.
beats.wrap: To sum up. [[w1]]Staff meetings: anything affecting more than two people; you moderate, you never lecture. [[w2]]Operation reviews teach across levels, and every player, audience included, has a job. [[w3]]Before calling a mission meeting: necessary, desirable, justifiable? [[w4]]Six or seven people, a clear agenda, punctual starts, fast minutes. [[w5]]Too many ad hoc meetings means the regular ones are not working. Now the lesson practice.
